message.content:
**Short answer:**  
Lions (*Panthera leo*) and zebras (*Equus quagga*, *E. grevyi* etc.) do **not** have a “recent” shared ancestor—each belongs to its own distinct branch of the mammalian tree. Their most‑recent common ancestor lived tens of millions of years ago as a very simple, generalized placental mammal that predated the major splits among modern land mammals.

---

### Where each species sits in the tree

| Taxon | Order | Family | Approximate age when it first appeared |
|-------|------|--------|----------------------------------------|
| Lion | Carnivora | Felidae | ≈ 25 Ma (Miocene) – earliest true cats appear later in the Miocene. |
| Zebra | Perissodactyla | Equidae | ≈ 20 Ma – horse‑like ungulates diversify in the Miocene. |

Both orders fall under the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**, which itself is nested inside the superorder **Euarchontoglires + Laurasiatheria** → **Theria** (placentals).

---

### Tracing back to the common ancestor

1. **Theryan origin**  
   - All placental mammals (“eutherians”) trace back to a single ancestral stock known as **Theria**. This group split off from marsupial and monotreme lineages sometime after the breakup of Pangaea, roughly **160–170 million years ago** (Late Jurassic/Early Cretaceous).

2. **Laurasiatherian diversification**  
   - Within Theria, the lineage leading to Carnivora (lions) and the lineage leading to Perissodactyla (zebras) separated during the **Early Cenozoic** (Paleocene), approximately **60–70 Myr ago**. These two branches represent deep divergences that produced entirely different body plans and ecological niches.

3. **Last common ancestor of lions & zebras**  
   - Because the two lineages branched so long ago, the last organism that gave rise to both is best described as a **small, insectivore‑to‑herbivore generalist placental mammal** existing in the **late Cretaceous to early Paleogene** (≈ 80–90 Myr ago). It had no obvious resemblance to either cat or horse today—it simply possessed the basic vertebrate anatomy characteristic of early mammals.

> **In plain terms:** Think of the common ancestor as a tiny, shrew‑ish creature roaming the forests of what will become North America or Eurasia over 85 million years ago. From this humble start, one descendant evolved into the sleek predator we know as the lion, while another took a completely different path toward becoming the striped herbivore we call the zebra.

---

### Why the question matters

When people ask “what’s the common ancestor?” they often expect a specific animal name (e.g., “the great ape”). In many cases—including lions and zebras—the answer isn’t a named species but rather a broad taxonomic category reflecting a very ancient branching point:

- **Common ancestor type:** Early placental mammal (theryan)
- **Time depth:** Roughly 80–95 million years ago
- **Significance:** Shows how diverse life forms can arise from a single primordial lineage through billions of years of evolution.

If you’re interested in even deeper roots, the ultimate common ancestor of all animals alive today dates back nearly 600 million years to the Cambrian explosion—a whole different story!
